title: ChatGPT Now Refuses to Write 'In the Style of' a Named Author
hook: Ask ChatGPT to imitate a living novelist and it will now decline — though Ars Technica reports it can still land on a suspiciously similar feeling if you describe the style instead.
key_points: OpenAI added a block on direct requests to copy a named author's writing style, per Ars Technica.
Describing the qualities you want — tone, rhythm, imagery — can still produce a similar result.
Style itself isn't clearly copyrightable; copying specific text is. The line is genuinely blurry.
The change reads as legal caution as much as ethics, with authors suing AI firms over training data.
Practical takeaway: 'write like X' prompts are on borrowed time; describe what you want instead.
content_html: OpenAI has started blocking one of the internet's favorite prompts: "write this in the style of [famous author]." Ars Technica reports ChatGPT now declines those direct requests — but if you describe the style's broad qualities instead, it can still land somewhere that feels awfully similar.
extra_html: The change matters less as a technical limit than as a signal. Copyright protects specific expression — the actual sentences someone wrote — not the harder-to-pin-down thing we call a voice or a style. That gap is unsettled law, and with authors and publishers already suing AI companies over how models were trained, guardrails like this look like a company deciding not to be the test case. For everyday users the practical lesson is simple: naming a writer is going out of fashion, but describing what you actually want — short sentences, dry humor, concrete detail — was always the better prompt anyway.

related.title: Who Owns AI's Output?
related.hook: You typed the prompt, the AI made the image — so who owns it? The law is genuinely unsettled, and the answer depends on where you are and how much was really you.

related.title: AI for Writing
related.hook: Writing is where AI earns its keep for most people: not replacing your voice, but beating the blank page, tightening drafts, and translating 'ugh' into a sendable email.

related.title: Can AI Be Creative?
related.hook: AI can write a poem or compose a tune that genuinely moves people. Whether that's 'real' creativity or very sophisticated remixing is a question with no settled answer — and it matters.

flashcards.prompt: What did OpenAI change about ChatGPT's handling of author styles?

choices.text: It now blocks direct requests to write in a named author's style
It now refuses to discuss authors at all
It now requires you to upload the author's books first

flashcards.explanation_html: Ars Technica reports ChatGPT started declining direct "write like [author]" requests — though describing the style's qualities can still get close.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'copying an author's style' legally murky rather than clearly illegal?
flashcards.back_html: Copyright protects specific expression — actual text — not a style or voice. So imitation sits in an unsettled gap, which is part of why companies are acting cautiously ahead of the courts.

flashcards.prompt: What's the practical workaround the article notes still works?

choices.text: Describing the qualities you want — tone, rhythm, imagery — rather than naming the author
Paying for a higher subscription tier

flashcards.explanation_html: The block targets the named-author request, not the underlying capability, so describing "broad qualities" can still capture a similar feeling.
